The maximum recorded fork length for Bigeye tuna (Thunnus obesus) is approximately 233 cm [Li = approximately 233 cm], a formidable size that makes it one of the larger tunas, though still somewhat smaller than the closely related Atlantic bluefin tuna. Achieving such an ultimate length requires many years of sustained growth, fueled by a highly active, warm-bodied physiology that allows this species to exploit deep, cooler waters during the day. Morphometric studies indicate this length is a conversion from measurements of total length, which can exceed 250 cm in the largest individuals, underscoring the substantial somatic investment required to reach the asymptotic size class. The species exhibits a fusiform body plan adapted for efficient cruising and burst swimming, with the fork length representing the standard metric for fisheries assessments and life-history comparisons across the genus Thunnus. This extraordinary ultimate size is rarely attained, as fishing mortality typically truncates the age structure of most populations, but in unexploited or lightly exploited stocks, individuals can approach this upper boundary, representing the culmination of decades of physiological performance and ecological success in the pelagic realm.

Reproductive maturation in Bigeye tuna is closely tied to size rather than age, with the onset of puberty occurring when individuals reach a fork length of approximately 105 cm [Lp = approximately 105 cm]. This length at maturity, which corresponds to roughly 45 percent of the ultimate length, is consistent with patterns observed in other large scombrids and suggests a life-history strategy that balances early reproduction against continued somatic growth. Field surveys and histological analyses of gonad development corroborate this value, although some regional variability exists, with estimates ranging from 100 to 125 cm depending on the population and the specific metric used, whether fork length or total length. Puberty marks the activation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis, initiating gametogenesis and the production of competent gametes. At this size, individuals begin their transition from the immature, growing phase to the reproductively active segment of the population, though the first successful spawning event may be deferred until slightly larger sizes are attained, a pattern common in iteroparous fishes.

At the warmer temperatures typical of tropical spawning aggregations (28.8 °C [T = 28.8 °C]), the embryonic period from fertilisation to hatching is remarkably brief, with eclosion occurring after approximately 0.88 days [ab = approximately 0.88 days]. This rapid developmental rate is an adaptation to the high predation pressure characteristic of the pelagic zone, where prolonged exposure as a yolk-sac larva would increase mortality substantially. The newly emerged, lecithotrophic larva measures only a few millimeters in length and carries a residual yolk supply that sustains it through the initial endotrophic phase. The wet weight at birth, based on the egg diameter of approximately 1.05 mm, is estimated at around 0.000606 grams [Wwb = around 0.000606 grams]. This extremely small initial mass reflects the considerable dilution of reproductive investment across a very high fecundity, a strategy that prioritises numerical output over per-offspring provisioning in a highly unpredictable larval environment where survival is determined largely by stochastic encounter rates with prey patches.

Under optimal thermal conditions of 20 °C [T = 20 °C], a mature female can release a substantial number of eggs per day. In natural terms, this translates to a maximum reproduction rate whereby a single female produces approximately 28,493 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 28,493 eggs per day] when maintained at 20 °C. This figure is derived from an annual fecundity of over 10 million eggs, partitioned across a protracted spawning season that may last several months in tropical and subtropical waters. The hydrated oocytes are released in multiple batches during serial spawning events, ensuring that gamete release coincides with periods of favourable oceanographic conditions for larval transport and prey availability. Such a prodigious fecundity is characteristic of large, pelagic scombrids and is a key factor in the species' demographic resilience, though it also implies a high degree of larval mortality, as only a tiny fraction of spawned eggs will survive to recruitment.

Longevity estimates for Bigeye tuna indicate a maximum lifespan of approximately 11 years [am = approximately 11 years] under natural conditions when the ambient water temperature is around 20 °C [T = 20 °C]. This lifespan, representing over a decade of active metabolism and growth, positions the species as a relatively long-lived member of the tuna complex, though shorter than the bluefin tunas which can exceed two decades. The ultimate wet weight attained by a fully grown adult is estimated at 210,000 grams [Wwi = 210,000 grams], representing an enormous increase from the sub-milligram larval mass at hatching, reflecting a growth trajectory of several orders of magnitude. This extraordinary biomass accumulation is sustained by a high-performance cardiovascular system and a diet of squid, crustaceans, and forage fishes. Age determination using otolith microchemistry and daily increment counts has validated these lifespans, though the oldest individuals in the wild are rarely encountered due to the intense fishing pressure that characterises modern tuna fisheries across the Pacific, Atlantic, and Indian Oceans.
